title: Supporting girls' retention: menstrual health and re-entry
description: A practical, sensitive guide for Kenyan school principals on helping girls stay in school, covering menstrual health, pregnancy and re-entry, and child protection.
body:
Some girls drop out or miss large amounts of school for reasons that schools can influence: lack of sanitary products, lack of privacy, pregnancy, and unsafe situations. A school that quietly removes these barriers keeps girls learning.

This subject needs care and confidentiality. The approach below focuses on support, dignity, and protection.

Menstrual health

Girls who cannot manage their periods at school often stay home. National policy supports provision of sanitary products in public schools, and schools should make sure the supply actually reaches girls and is available discreetly.

  • Private washrooms with water and a place to dispose of used products.
  • A discreet point of support, such as a trusted female teacher or matron, where girls can get products without embarrassment.
  • Plain, respectful health education for girls and boys, so that periods are not a source of teasing.

Pregnancy and return to school

Ministry of Education guidelines support the return of girls to school after pregnancy. A school with a clear, supportive re-entry process, without stigma, helps a girl complete her education. Counselling, flexibility in the weeks around birth, and a welcoming class teacher make a real difference.

Confidentiality builds trust: Girls will only come forward if they believe their situation will be handled privately and without blame. Share information only with those who need it to help.

Protect: pregnancy can signal abuse

When a young girl becomes pregnant, the school has a duty to consider whether she has been abused, and to follow child protection procedures. Do not handle this as a matter of discipline. Involve the guidance and counselling teacher, follow the reporting channels, and seek help from the relevant authorities. Verified helplines include Childline Kenya on 116 and the national GBV helpline on 1195. Confirm current numbers locally.

Notice the signs early

Watch for patterns: a girl who is regularly absent on certain days, whose grades drop suddenly, or who withdraws from friends. A quiet, private conversation is usually more effective than a public question.
